summary:
FireLens is an interactive decision-support application that transforms NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations into one comparable fire-activity record. Because the satellites have different resolutions and sensitivities, their raw hotspot counts cannot be compared directly. FireLens harmonizes them using common 5 km active grid-cell days and transparent calibration derived from overlapping observations.

Users can explore fire history from 2000 through October 2026, compare raw and harmonized trends, investigate unusual months, view mapped activity, and select and download compiled monthly data for further analysis or operational reporting. FireLens also evaluates its seasonal predictions against 46 later observed months and provides a low-confidence December 2026 planning outlook.

By compiling complex satellite records into accessible calendars, maps, forecasts, and downloadable datasets, FireLens helps emergency planners, scientists, and land managers identify periods requiring closer attention without mistaking changes in satellite technology for changes in real-world burning.
details:
FireLens is an interactive decision-support application that combines NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into one comparable historical record. MODIS and VIIRS have different resolutions and sensitivities, so directly joining their raw hotspot counts can create misleading changes when the satellite record transitions between sensors. FireLens addresses this problem by placing detections on a common 5 km grid and counting an active grid-cell day as one Fire Activity Unit. Month-specific calibration factors derived from overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations make the older and newer records more comparable.

The application allows users to explore burning activity from November 2000 through October 2026. Its Fire Rhythm Calendar reveals seasonal patterns, extreme months, and long-term changes. Selecting a month updates the activity metrics, historical percentile, responder-oriented explanation, and map. Users can switch between raw detections and harmonized activity to see why harmonization matters. They can also compile and download monthly results as a CSV file for further research, reporting, or operational analysis.

FireLens includes a historical replay of September 2020, which reached the 100th historical percentile and was approximately 774% above the historical September median. Its forecasting component was trained using information available through 2022 and evaluated against 46 later observed months from 2023 through October 2026. The model achieved a mean absolute error of approximately 139 Fire Activity Units. FireLens also provides a low-confidence December 2026 planning outlook/prediction while clearly separating predictions from observed activity and excluding incomplete November data.

The intended impact is to help emergency planners, scientists, firefighters, and land managers recognize periods requiring closer attention, understand where detected activity was concentrated, prepare for historically active periods, and access compiled evidence for additional analysis. FireLens supports human decision-making; it does not issue evacuation orders, predict individual fires, or replace official emergency information.

The frontend was developed with React, TypeScript, Vite, React-Leaflet, Recharts, HTML, and CSS. Python was used to clean, aggregate, harmonize, validate, and export the NASA data. The application uses static JSON, CSV, and GeoJSON assets, OpenStreetMap basemaps, Vitest for automated testing, GitHub for version control, and Vercel for public deployment.

FireLens is creative because it does more than display hotspots. It exposes the sensor-transition problem, lets users compare raw and corrected records, turns decades of observations into an accessible activity calendar, tests predictions against later observations, maps historical activity, and makes the processed results downloadable. The team prioritized scientific transparency, accessibility, colorblind-safe visualization, responsive design, data quality, reproducibility, and reliable public access. Important limitations including clouds, satellite overpass timing, incomplete observation coverage, provisional near-real-time data, and the distinction between hotspot pixels and actual fire boundaries are displayed directly in the application.
